reports.gin-14dd7940711f:
I registered a couple of routes where a parameter is followed by a fixed segment, and then requested the same path with a trailing slash:

```go
router.GET("/hello/:name", handler)
router.GET("/hello/:name/123", handler)

// client requests: GET /hello/abx/
```

I expected the router to notice that `/hello/abx` exists and answer with a redirect to the version without the trailing slash, the way it does for plain paths. Instead the request just came back as a 404, with no redirect and no hint that the slash was the problem. It's confusing because the same trailing-slash request works fine for routes that don't have a parameter in that position.
reports.gin-6df8c584a613:
I turned on `HandleMethodNotAllowed` and registered a group with a few wildcard routes, then requested a URL that doesn't match any of them. I expected a plain 404, but the server crashed with a runtime "index out of range" panic instead.

```go
r := gin.New()
r.HandleMethodNotAllowed = true

base := r.Group("/base")
v1 := base.Group("/v1")
v1.GET("/:id/devices", handler)
v1.GET("/user/:id/groups", handler)
v1.GET("/orgs/:id", handler)
v1.DELETE("/orgs/:id", handler)

// GET /base/v1/user/groups -> panic instead of 404
```

With `HandleMethodNotAllowed` left at its default, the same request correctly returns 404, so it only breaks when that option is enabled.
reports.gin-894d294a5419:
I'm serving a download whose filename comes from user input, and I noticed the quotes and backslashes in it end up in the response header exactly as I passed them:

```go
c.FileAttachment("./report.pdf", `evil"; dummy="x.sh`)
```

I expected the filename to be escaped so the header still contains a single, well-formed filename, but instead the raw quotes and backslashes are written straight through, producing something like `attachment; filename="evil"; dummy="x.sh"`. Any client or intermediary reading that header sees extra parameters I never set, which is a real problem when the filename isn't fully under my control.
reports.gin-97ac74ce652b:
When a client sends an `Accept` header that starts with one of the formats I offer but has extra characters at the end, my server crashes instead of just not matching.

```go
c.Request.Header.Set("Accept", "image/tiff-fx")
format := c.NegotiateFormat("image/tiff")
```

I expected `NegotiateFormat` to return an empty string, since `image/tiff-fx` is not the same as `image/tiff`. Instead the request panicked with `runtime error: index out of range [10] with length 10`.
reports.gin-a840d8b56d38:
I set up my router with `RedirectFixedPath = true` and registered a static route and a parameter route under the same prefix. When I request the path with different casing or with extra segments, the server panics with `invalid node type` instead of redirecting to the static route or returning a 404. I expected `/PREFIX/XXX` to redirect to `/prefix/xxx`, and `/prefix/a/b/c` to simply 404.

```go
r.RedirectFixedPath = true
r.GET("/prefix/:id", handler)
r.GET("/prefix/xxx", handler)
// request /PREFIX/XXX or /prefix/a/b/c -> panic: invalid node type
```
reports.gin-af4e235f3b3e:
I set the `X-Forwarded-Prefix` header to values that contain special characters like `#`, `?`, `%`, or `:`, and then requested a path that triggers a trailing-slash redirect. For example:

```go
req := httptest.NewRequest("GET", "/path/", nil)
req.Header.Set("X-Forwarded-Prefix", "#bug")
```

I expected the redirect `Location` header to contain the prefix safely encoded so the browser would go to the correct URL. Instead the redirect came back with a malformed or incorrectly escaped location, and the browser ended up at the wrong address. This happens whenever the prefix includes characters that have special meaning in a URL.
reports.gin-ba43554592c5:
In a middleware I copy the request context so I can use it after the handler returns:

```go
cp := c.Copy()
go func() {
    log.Println(cp.FullPath())
}()
```

I expected `cp.FullPath()` to return the same matched route as `c.FullPath()` (for example `/users/:id`), but the copy always logs an empty string. The original context still reports the correct path, so the copy is losing it.
reports.gin-e4b29bb10696:
I'm wrapping one of the library's error values (not a pointer) with `fmt.Errorf` and then trying to match the original error through it, but the match fails:

```go
err := Error{Err: innerErr, Type: ErrorTypeAny}
wrapped := fmt.Errorf("wrapped: %w", err)

errors.Is(wrapped, innerErr) // false, I expected true
var target TestErr
errors.As(wrapped, &target)  // false, I expected true
```

The same code works when I wrap a pointer to the error instead, so I expected the value form to behave identically. Instead both checks silently report that the wrapped error isn't there at all.
reports.gin-ee42fee2b029:
I set the status to 200 and flushed the response, then later code tried to set it to 401. I expected the original 200 to remain because the response had already been sent, but calling `Status()` afterward returned 401. The client still received 200, so my logs and metrics now report a status that was never actually sent.

```go
w.WriteHeader(http.StatusOK)
w.WriteHeaderNow()

// later, after the response is already sent
w.WriteHeader(http.StatusUnauthorized)
fmt.Println(w.Status()) // got 401, expected 200
```
